On another day too, that very powerful hawk arrived;
he remained there facing the two of them for two watches.
Looking at their way once more, he quickly departed as he had come.
When that bird had gone, she spoke to the winged one:
“Lord, let us go to another place; Death has surely approached nearby.
If he is seen again, our dwelling and our happiness will be destroyed, my love!
Beloved, for one whose flight of wings brings success everywhere,
would such a wise one perish through attachment to his own place?
He who, having abandoned his troubled homeland, does not go to another,
that crippled man meets destruction, like a tree standing on a riverbank.”
Hearing what his beloved said, he, driven by the power of destiny,
spoke to her again: “My love, tormented by fear of the bird, do not be afraid!”
And on the next day, that hawk, very early in the morning,
reached the entrance of the nest and remained motionless until evening.

6.2.m:
When the sun went to the crest of the setting mountain and the bird had departed,
the female pigeon came outside the nest and said to her husband:
“Lord, this is the time for departure; Death is at a distance.
Flee as best you can, even leaving me, the warning one, behind!
While you are alive, nothing on earth is unobtainable.
Wives can be had again, sons again, wealth again, and a home again.
If a man preserves himself even at the cost of wives and wealth,
then everything is regained, as by King Hariścandra.
One's self is the dearest kinsman, one's self is the greatest wealth;
this self is the supreme acquirer of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
As long as there is safety for oneself, so long is there safety in the three worlds.
Even that safety is desired along with a good destination and fame;
but rather than safety devoid of fame, death is better than that safety.
That fame is gained by men who conduct themselves in the path of prudence;
therefore, ponder the path of prudence, lord: depart from this place!

Though thus addressed by his wife, the very wise female pigeon,
he did not depart from that place, restrained by destiny.
Then at dawn, arriving there, that mighty hawk,
having eaten something, blocked the exit doorway.
The very powerful hawk remained there for a few days,
and said this to the pigeon: “Fie on you, devoid of manly courage!
Either fight, evil-minded one, or come out at my command!
Wasted by hunger, dead afterwards, you will surely see hell!”
Fate indeed would not help you; [this was] not spoken [in vain]."
Addressed thus by the hawk, that bird, accompanied by his wife,

Hungry and thirsty, he was then seized by the mighty hawk
with a firm claw swiftly, and that female bird was also seized by the beak.
Taking both of them, the hawk quickly flew into the sky,

Then Kalarava was addressed there by his highly intelligent wife:
"Since I was despised by you, O lord, thinking 'She is a woman,'
therefore you have reached this state; what can I do, since I am a weak woman?
Even now, O dear one, if you carry out one word of mine,
then I shall tell you what is beneficial; do it without hesitation.
By carrying out one word of mine you will not become one conquered by a woman.
As long as I have [only] entered his mouth, and as long as he is in the sky and not on the ground,
so long, for your own release, bite his foot firmly with your beak!"
Hearing his wife's word, that bird did so.
Hard pressed in the foot, the hawk shrieked loudly.
With that screeching, she was released from his open beak;
and when the toes of his claws loosened, that pigeon also fell.
Even in misfortune, effort must never be abandoned by the wise.
Where was the tip of his beak, and where was the grasping of that foot?

6.2.m:
And where was the miraculous deliverance of the two from afar in such a manner?
"Even for the weak, effort is better"—so it is sung in the scriptures.
Therefore, according to destiny, effort always bears fruit;
and hence the wise praise effort even in misfortune. / Then the two died in the course of time at Jambūmārga;
for those who die at Jambūmārga, heaven is ever imperishable.
Then, through the residue of merit, an auspicious son of a gandharva was born,
the son of Mandāradāman, named Parimalālaya.
A repository of many sciences, an abode of skill in the arts,
having attained youthful age, he became devoted to bhakti for Śiva.
With conquered senses and mind, he also undertook a vow:
"I will constantly practice the vow of fidelity to a single wife"—this was his resolve.
Attachment to another's wife steals away life, fame, strength, happiness,
and even going to heaven; therefore, a wise man should avoid it.

as long as the body is free from disease, as long as there is no affliction of the senses,
so long must Trilocana be revered in Avanti; of this there is no doubt."
Thus that son of Mandāradāman, Parimalālaya, in Kāśī
would diligently come every day to see Trilocana.
The female pigeon was also born in the house of Ratnadīpa,
the king of the nāgas in Pātāla, by the name of Ratnāvalī.
Among all the nāga maidens, by her beauty, good character, arts, and virtues,
that daughter of the serpent Ratnadīpa alone was like a jewel.
She had two female companions, one named Prabhāvatī,
and the other Kalāvatī; both were auspicious and constantly attended her.
Never parting from her body, like shadow and radiance,
those two were former friends of Ratnāvalī, O Maheśvarī.

"O father, having worshipped Trilocana day after day in Kāśī
accompanied by these two companions, I shall break my silence, not otherwise."
Thus that nāga maiden, accompanied by her two companions,
having worshipped Trilocana, would return home day after day.
Wreathing very diverse garlands of fresh, very auspicious flowers
with delightful fragrances, she would worship the all-pervading Lord.
All three sang song charmingly and with sweet voices;
with movements of a women's dance-circle, all three also performed gentle dance,
skilled in tempo and rhythm with the vīṇā, flute, and mṛdaṅga.
played [them] joyfully, and then all three came to rest.
Thus the three Nāga maidens worshipped the Lord,
worshipping the Three-eyed One with a series of diverse figures.
Having bathed in the morning of the fourth lunar day in the auspicious Pilipila tīrtha,
and then worshipped the Three-eyed One, they fell fast asleep in the performance hall.

6.2.m:
While they were asleep, Śiva, the three-eyed one adorned with the moon,
whose left half shone with his Śakti, who wore a serpent as a sacred thread,
having indeed emerged from the liṅga itself, girdled with the Gaṅgā and serpents,
the all-pervading Lord spoke to the maidens, saying, “Arise!”
Arising and rubbing their eyes that reached to their ears,
stretching their limbs and rolling their eyes,
as they looked before them with bewildered minds,
just then they beheld the Three-eyed One, whose arrival was unthought of.
Then those young women bowed, recognizing the Lord by his distinguishing marks,
and filled with joy, their voices choked with emotion, they praised him in deep agitation:
“Victory to Śambhu! Victory to Īśāna! Victory to the omnipresent one, the giver of everything!
Victory to the destroyer of Tripura! Victory to the slayer of Andhaka!
Victory to the destroyer of Jalandhara! Victory to the vanquisher of the pride of the god of love!
Victory to the creator of the three worlds! Victory to the one venerated by the three worlds!
Victory to the lord of devotees! Victory to the leader of the Pramathas!
Homage to you, homage to you, homage to you, reverence again and again!

Having spoken thus, the maidens fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff.
Then, raising those young women up, the moon-adorned Lord spoke:
“The son of Mandāradāman, named Parimalālaya,
an eminent Vidyādhara, shall become your husband.
Having enjoyed pleasures on every side for a long time in the world of the Vidyādharas,
then reaching Avantikā and meditating upon me, you will attain perfection.
In a previous life as well, devotion was paid to me by you and by him;
by virtue of that, your birth is spotless, suffused with devotion.
Those who recite this Prabhāvatī hymn in front of me,
to them I shall grant their desires; this is the boon granted to you.”
When the Lord of gods had spoken thus, those maidens, their minds rejoicing,
bowed down and addressed Īśāna with their palms folded together:
The Nāga maidens said:
“We ask: tell us, O Lord, compassionate Śaṃkara,
how was service rendered to you by the four of us in a previous birth?

Hearing this desired request voiced with affection by the young women,

The Lord said:
“Listen attentively, all three Nāga daughters:
I shall recount the previous life of yourselves and of him.
Formerly, this Ratnāvalī was a female pigeon, a bird;
and that eminent Vidyādhara was her husband, a bird.
And happily they resided for a very long time in my temple;
the dust adhering to the temple was continually driven off by the wind of their wings.
Numerous circumambulations were made above and below;
and moving through the air, they frequented my courtyard.
They bathed at the Caturnada tīrtha and drank the water there repeatedly;
and softly cooing, sweet sounds were joyfully made by these two.

Owing to the condition of animal birth, they did not die in my presence;
since they died on the Jambū path, which surely brings the attainment of heaven,

gave them to Nārāyaṇa, the son of Āmuṣyāyaṇa.

and there in the woods, through the power of fate, he was bitten by a serpent.
Those two daughters of Cārāyaṇa, named Bhavānī and Gautamī,
befallen by the grief of widowhood, were seized with misery.
Therefore, a wise man who is to marry should carefully avoid
taking the hand of a maiden named after a goddess or a river.
Then, by chance, in the god-like hermitage of a certain sage,
out of delusion they took plantain fruits that had not been given.
Having observed various fasts and other observances, the two daughters of the brahmin
met their death in the course of time and became female monkeys.
Through the ripening of the theft of fruit, they obtained the state of monkeys;
by virtue of preserving their virtue, they attained birth in Avantī.
And that brahmin Nārāyaṇa, devoted to serving his father,
though bitten by the serpent, became a pigeon in Kāśī.
Thus, in another birth he was indeed the husband of both of them;
and he will again be the husband of you three.
At the side of the palace was a great banyan tree;

In play, they dipped into the water of the sacred ford Viṣṇudeha;
and afflicted by thirst, they also drank the water in that sacred ford.
Playing out of the natural restlessness of their species,
they circumambulated it many times and gazed at the liṅga often.
While roaming freely here and there in the vicinity of that banyan tree,
they were captured with a noose by someone in the guise of an ascetic.
They were trained by him to [help him] beg alms; there was no leaping or returning.
Then somewhere those two female monkeys succumbed to the law of time.
By the merit of dwelling in Avantī, by their service to Trilocana,
and according to their circumambulations, the two were born as daughters of serpents.
Now, having obtained that vidyādhara youth as husband,
and having enjoyed the pleasures of heaven, you will attain liberation in Avantī.
Whatever auspicious deed, even a small one, is performed in Avantī,
its ultimate fruit is certainly liberation through my grace.

In the entire three worlds, the city of Avantī is ever supreme;
even more than it, the Omkāra liṅga; and even more than that, Trilocana here.
Abiding in this liṅga, I indeed bestow worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Therefore, with every effort Trilocana is to be worshipped in Avantī.”
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods of gods entered inside that temple,
assuming the form of the liṅga, auspicious beyond the three worlds.
They, having reached their own home, recounted that entire account
before their mother, feeling as though their purpose were fulfilled.
Once, in the month of Mādhava, caravans arrived together;
the vidyādharas and the serpents assembled with their retinues
in the great sacred field free from dust, near Trilocana.
And because of the god's bestowal of the boon, having inquired of each other's lineages,
those three maidens were assigned by the serpents to the vidyādhara.
Mandāradāman was delighted, having obtained that triad of daughters-in-law.

Those kinsmen, their eyes blooming with joy at one another,
arranged the wedding festival and entered their respective dwellings,
extolling the majesty of the Trilocana liṅga.
And that glorious Vidyādhara, [having enjoyed] abundant happiness with the serpent maidens,
having enjoyed [it], then went to Avantī and worshipped Trilocana.
Singing an exceedingly sweet song together with the serpent maidens, the accomplished one,
having completely forgotten himself, attained dissolution in the middle of the liṅga.
The majesty of Trilocana was hidden by the god in the Kali age;
therefore, men of little virtue do not worship that liṅga.
Oh, having heard this story of Trilocana, even a mortal joined with sin
becomes free from sin and attains the supreme state.
This power that destroys sin has been told to you, O goddess;
hear [now] of the supreme Vīreśvara of Lord Trilocana.

Glorious Hara said:
Now hear, O goddess, of the forty-sixth, Vīreśvara,
by the mere sight of which the increase of one's lineage surely occurs.
Listen attentively to the supreme appearance of the great Vīreśa,
upon hearing which, O Śivā, the ancestors obtain abundant merit.
There was a king named Amitrajit, a conqueror of enemy cities,
righteous, endowed with goodness, intent on delighting his subjects,
whose wealth was fame, generous, wise, regarding brahmins as gods,
whose hair was constantly wet from bathing at the conclusion of sacrifices,
modest, endowed with policy, skilled in all duties,
learned in sciences, virtuous, affectionate to the virtuous,
grateful, speaking sweetly, averse to sinful acts,
truthful, an abode of purity, speaking truth, his senses mastered,
a veritable god of death on the field of battle, discerning in assembly,
knowing the right time for sport with lovely women, beloved of elders though young,
whose treasury of wealth was for righteousness, with well-equipped forces and vehicles,
fortunate, handsome, of noble intellect, dear to good subjects,
endowed with steadfastness and courage, discerning place and time,
always showing honor to those worthy of honor, free from all blemishes.
Having placed the disposition of his mind upon the two feet of Vāsudeva,
he ruled the kingdom without dispute and free from reproaches.
His command unassailable, the glorious one, devoted to devotion to Viṣṇu,
enjoyed excellent pleasures all around that were purified by Viṣṇu.
In every palace, at every step, high acts of worship to Hari
took place in the kingdom of that treasure-house of great good fortune, O Śivā:
'O enchanter of the herds of cows, cowherds, boys, and gopīs!
O mace-bearer! Beyond attributes, yet full of virtues! O Garuḍa-bannered Lord!
O slayer of Keśin! Enemy of Kaiṭabha! Foe of Kaṃsa! Lord of Kamalā!
O Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, lotus-eyed, destroyer of the fear of death!
O Supreme Person, foe of sin, lotus-eyed!
Clothed in yellow silk, lotus-naveled, higher than the highest!
Janārdana, Lord of the world, birthplace of the waters of the Jāhnavī!
Remover of rebirth for living beings, destroyer of the host of sins!
With the Śrīvatsa on your chest, beautiful-necked, bestower of prosperity, treasure of blessings!
Śrīraṅga, bearer of the Śārṅga bow, descendant of Śūra, moon-eyed!
Enemy of Daityas! Foe of Dānavas! Dāmodara! Slayer of Duraṃtaka!
Joy of Devakī's heart! Sleeper upon the lord of serpents!
O Viṣṇu! Dweller in Vaikuṇṭha! Foe of Bāṇa! All-hearing one!
Viṣvaksena! Omnipresent! Hero! Wearing the forest garland! Dear to Bali!
Trivikrama! Lord of the three worlds! Discus-bearer! Four-armed!' —
Such sacred names in every temple,
uttered by the mouths of women, the aged, children, and cowherds,
the charming names of the foe of Madhu were heard everywhere.
Delightful pleasure-groves were seen in every home.
Wondrous deeds were sung in every home,
and elaborate paintings were seen on the palace walls.
Apart from talk of Hari, no other report was heard.
Deer were never slain by lions, nor flesh-bearing deer
by hunters roaming at ease in the forest, out of fear of that king.

Īśvara said:
Know the fifty-third well-renowned lord,
The supreme Viśveśvara, famed throughout all the worlds.
Formerly in Vidarbhā, there was a king named Vidūratha.
Endowed with ten thousand women in his inner quarters, he ruled an undisputed kingdom.
Then, having gone hunting, through heedlessness he slew an ascetic
Wearing a black antelope skin, peaceful, meditating upon the eternal Brahman.
Deluded by destiny in the great forest, mistaking the brahmin for a deer, [he killed him].
By that ripening of karma, at the end of his body he went to the Raurava hell.
Having experienced dreadful torment there according to his appointed time,
He came here to the mortal realm from there and became a venomous serpent.
He bit a brahmin on the foot in anger, O beloved.
Struck by a club, he too met his death at that very instant.
Falling from hell, in his second birth he became a terrifying lion.
He devoured a king and was struck down by the royal guards.

6.2.m: Īśvara said: / Know the fifty-seventh, and now hear about Ghaṇṭeśvara, / By the mere darśana of whom the attainment of desires takes place. // There was an excellent gaṇa named Ghaṇṭa, who was dear to me. / In the period of the Manu Cākṣuṣa, for sport and at his own whim, / He set out for the abode of Brahmā to see the imperishable Brahmā. // Then, seeing the gandharva Citrasena who was skilled in singing approaching, / The best of gaṇas joyfully inquired after his well-being: // “I must go right there to the abode of the Supreme Lord; / With songs I shall worship Brahmā, the lord of the worlds.” // Citrasena then replied to him, O goddess, and said to Ghaṇṭa: / “The lotus-born [Brahmā] has undertaken secret counsel with the gods.” // Having heard this, the gaṇa Ghaṇṭa stood with a bewildered mind. / Turned away by the door-keeper, he reflected for a moment: // “Abandoning the master Īśāna, I have come to see Brahmā; / Even entry cannot be obtained, and favor remains far off.” // While he was thus reflecting, a full year passed; / Ghaṇṭa did not obtain entry at the door of Brahmā, O goddess. // Then, seeing Nārada with a vīṇā in hand, eager, / Coming out from inside the house of the lotus-born [Brahmā], that best of gaṇas, / Ghaṇṭa quickly addressed him: “Announce me, O Nārada! // I am a gaṇa knowing the truth of song, beloved of Mahādeva; / I have arrived for the darśana of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.” // Having heard Ghaṇṭa’s words, the sage was pleased; / Consoling him deceitfully, Nārada replied with this: // “I have been sent to the presence of Bṛhaspati, O leader of gaṇas, / By Brahmā, the creator of the world, to ask about some other business. / I will return in just a moment; wait for that long!” // Having spoken thus, O goddess, Nārada came to my presence; / That best of sages recounted the story of Ghaṇṭa: // “A servant like Ghaṇṭa is hard to find, O Lord! / The gaṇa who, having left you, O Lord, for the service of the Supreme Lord, / Stood for a full year and did not obtain entrance!”

6.2.m:
Having heard those words of that sage Nārada at that time,
He was cursed by me in anger: “Fall to the earth, O Ghaṇṭa!
For, having abandoned me, you went elsewhere to another’s house for service.”
And when that word was uttered by me, even though he was standing at the door of Brahmā,
Ghaṇṭa fell onto the earth near the Devadāru forest.
Seeing himself fallen on the ground, O Pārvatī, by Ghaṇṭa
A speech full of grief was uttered in faltering words:
“He who, abandoning his own lord, goes elsewhere for service,
Goes to a terrible hell and finds disrepute.
By Nārada, both have been lost today for me who was deceived,
Since neither Brahmā is my master, nor the god Maheśvara.”
While he was lamenting in this way, Nārada, the best of sages,
Came to that spot where Ghaṇṭa was staying
In the Devadāru forest, O goddess, to see the ascetics.
Nārada was seen by Ghaṇṭa, who was afraid and confused in mind:
“Having reduced me to such a state, what else will he do to me?”

6.2.m:
To him who was reflecting in this manner, Nārada spoke these words:
“O leader of gaṇas, you should not harbor anger, which destroys merit.
You have fallen for the sake of fame, O Ghaṇṭa, and solely for the sake of expiation.
With your soul purified by expiation, you will attain the lord Śaṃkara.
Therefore, by my instruction, go to the auspicious forest of Mahākāla.
To the east of Revanteśvara, there exists an excellent liṅga,
Bestowing all prosperity, celestial; it will attain renown through your name.”
Having been thus addressed by Nārada, Jaigīṣavya arrived;
By him too it was all told: “Truth indeed has been spoken by him,
By Nārada, O leader of gaṇas; your fame will become imperishable.
by Kaśyapa, Mṛkaṇḍu, Kaṇva, Jamadagni,
Atri, Bhṛgu, O goddess, and Lomaśa, the celestial seer.
Thus addressed, Ghaṇṭa went swiftly to the auspicious forest of Mahākāla,
where, by the ringing of a bell as I fought in battle,
an excellent liṅga arose, O goddess, which destroys sins.

Being pleased, narrated the supreme māhātmya of the liṅga.
Indra said:
"In the Mahākālavana forest there is a liṅga established of old by Brahmā,
Possessing a divine form, celestial, to the east of the venerable Siddheśvara.
Merely by its darśana you will attain the status of a brahmin."
Then, in accordance with Vāsava's word, Mataṅga went
To the delightful Mahākālavana forest, that incomparable sacred field of perfections.
There he saw that liṅga which grants all fruits.
Having seen it, he worshipped it with various kinds of flowers.
Being worshipped, that best of gods replied thus to Mataṅga:
"Ah, you are greatly fortunate, since I have been pleased by you.
From me arose the whole universe, the earth, mid-region, and the rest.
I am the granter of boons to those who deserve boons, and the giver of curses to the wicked.
By my grace your status as a brahmin shall be imperishable."
Then Mataṅga attained the status of a brahmin by the darśana of the liṅga;
Furthermore, by the power of worship, he went to the world of Brahmā, O twice-born one.
The rarely attained status of a brahmin was obtained through the power of this liṅga
By Mataṅga, O fair-waisted one; therefore the god is celebrated
In the world as Mataṅgeśvara, the bestower of the world of Brahmā.
Hostile to the classes and stages of life, delighting in heretical words,
Deceitful, unethical, shameless, and exceedingly greedy,
Pitiless, doing cruel deeds, insolent men in the Kali age—
Even they go to heaven by the darśana of that liṅga.
Those who are purified, highly fortunate, contemplative, and destined for liberation,
They behold Īśvara as Mataṅgeśvara in the Kali age, O goddess.
Those who are intent on meditation on Brahman, and devoted to sacrifices and acts of giving,
They behold Īśvara as Mataṅgeśvara in the Kali age, O goddess.
Those who worship Īśvara as Mataṅgeśvara, O great goddess—

6.2.m:
Īśvara said: / Know the sixty-first [liṅga] to be Saubhāgyeśvara, / by the mere darśana of which one obtains matchless good fortune.
Formerly, in the natural kalpa, there was a king named Aśvavāhana, / righteous, renowned, in the pleasant city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Wise, the performer of many sacrifices, undefeated in battles. / His wife, O large-eyed one, was named Madanamañjarī.
The fair-browed daughter of the king of Kāśi, exceedingly beautiful in appearance, / clever, virtuous, most righteous, skilled in household duties,
endowed with sixty-four arts, always devoted to her husband's welfare, / with a face like the full moon, gentle, and always sweetly speaking.
O goddess, by the force of past deeds she became unloved [by her husband]. / She was disliked by that king, always distressing his eyes.
Her speech caused torment to the king's ears; / the sight of her always burned the king's eyes.
At her touch, that king would fall into an unbearable faint. / Once, looked upon with love by her, O fair-faced one,
burning with an intense fire, the king uttered these words:
"Gatekeeper, take this unfortunate wife and in the deep forest / abandon her immediately; do not question this order of mine!"
Then, seeing that the king's command was not to be questioned, / the gatekeeper placed that fair-browed lady in a chariot and abandoned her in the forest.
Abandoned in the deserted forest, weeping again and again, / she remembered that king; she considered him her deity.
Then she, beautiful in every limb, her mind fixed upon him, / spent the remainder of the day and the night given over to deep sighs.
Sighing, her limbs flawless, weeping repeatedly, "Alas, alas!" / the intoxicating-eyed lady reproached herself as ill-fated.
Neither in diversion, nor in food, nor in that charming forest, / nor in the caves of the mountains did she then find delight.

6.2.m:
Abandoned by him, O lady of fair hips, she cursed her own youth:
"Subdued by wicked fate, why was I born here so unfortunate? / How was such an excellent king obtained by me as my husband?
Blessed is he, of great merit, who is the object of this youth, / and who will doubtless take pleasure with other, unchaste women!
To one man a wife is dear; to another woman a husband is desired. / A wedlock rich in mutual love is exceedingly rare.
This king is dear to me, but I am not dear to the king. / Mutual affection indeed arises only for the blessed.
If that king does not unite with me today, / then the unbearable fire of desire will surely consume me.
That forest, which was charming and resounding with male cuckoos, / now seems to burn me, bereft of my beloved."
Thus possessed by passion, lamenting again and again, / she saw an ascetic there, a knower of the three times, firm in vows,
subsisting on a girdle, a deer skin, a loincloth, a staff, and firewood, / of great splendor, highly fortunate, desiring liberation, the best of sages,
resembling the rising sun, shining like fire. / Seeing him, that queen, thought ill of [by her husband] though virtuous, rose up at once.
Subduing herself with modesty, having prostrated and greeted him, / bowing low, the chaste woman asked the cause of separation from the king:
"O venerable one, I am the daughter of the king of Kāśi, exceedingly beloved, / sister of Śatrusena, and very dear to my mother.
Married by the king named Aśvavāhana, O great sage, / in accordance with righteousness, by a righteous rite, one equal to Prajāpati.
Why then have I become disliked by that king, / while he, the monarch, is always exceedingly dear to me, O lord?
How did I become unfortunate? By what deed, O ascetic? / How can my husband, the best of kings, become subservient to me, / and how may good fortune be mine? Tell me this truthfully!"

6.2.m:
Hearing her words, the sage of strict vows / explained to her through his insight the cause of her ill fortune:
“At the moment of marriage, you were aspected by malefic planets; / your husband, the king, O daughter, was aspected by benefic planets.
Therefore the king is dear to you, but you are not dear to the king.” / Hearing his words, the queen, despondent in mind,
inquired with humility, bowing her neck in devotion:
“O venerable one, by what gift, by what ritual ablution, and by what observance, / by what deed indeed may supreme good fortune come to be?”
Hearing her words, the sage of strict vows / recounted the māhātmya by which good fortune is attained:
“In the Mahākāla forest, O daughter, is a liṅga that bestows good fortune; / beside Mataṅgeśvara, it grants what is desired.
Merely by the darśana of it, you will obtain good fortune.
That liṅga was formerly worshipped by Indrāṇī for the sake of good fortune; / she obtained supreme good fortune, and even Indra, who was lost, was regained by her.
Therefore, go by my command to the auspicious Mahākāla forest.
Good fortune will be yours there, as well as a meeting with your beloved; / an auspicious son will be born from the darśana of that liṅga.”
Having been spoken to thus by that ascetic, O fair-faced one, / she went to the Mahākāla forest where that liṅga is located.
Filled with affection, she beheld the liṅga that bestows good fortune. / From the darśana of that liṅga, the king remembered his beloved wife.
He asked Jamadagni: “O lord, where has my beloved gone? / Has she been devoured in the forest, O brahmin, by lions, tigers, or night-wandering demons?
She was abandoned by me, a cruel man, yet I was dear to her.” / As the king spoke thus, he was answered by Jamadagni:
“She has not been devoured, O ruler of the earth, by lions, tigers, or night-wandering demons. / Her conduct is uncorrupted; she is devoted to you and faithful to her husband.

6.2.m:
She has gone to the Mahākāla forest, O king, desiring good fortune. / A wife must be protected, O ruler of the earth: so states the supreme Vedic scripture.
When a wife is protected, offspring are protected; / for the self is born in her, therefore she must be protected, O lord of men.
A loss of virtue occurs day by day for one without a wife, O king; / there is failure in daily rites, and that surely leads to downfall.
A wife should be accommodating, whatever the nature of the husband; / even a ill-natured or unfortunate wife must be maintained, O lord of men.”
Hearing his words, the ruler of men arrived / in the delightful Mahākāla forest and then beheld his beloved,
adorned with good fortune, the fair-browed one worshiping Maheśvara. / Seeing her, embracing her with affection, he spoke in return to that beloved:
“I have been tormented by separation from you, O fair-faced one. / Today my eyes are fruitful, and my life is truly a good life,
since I see you, O fortunate lady; I have been made fulfilled by you.” / Having seen her husband thus with great joy, / she said, “Be gracious,” again and again, filled with delight.
Then the king, having embraced the lovely lady with impetuosity, said: / “Beloved, I am already gracious; what more should I say repeatedly?”
Then their union took place, and an exceedingly virtuous son was born; / by the māhātmya of that liṅga, he is celebrated by the name Datta.
Incomparable good fortune was attained by that queen, O daughter of Himavat; / from that time forward on the surface of the earth, it has been known as Saubhāgyeśvara.
Those who behold the lord Saubhāgyeśvara, O wide-eyed lady, / in their family ill fortune is not born, O daughter of the mountain.
There will be no poverty, and no separation from kinsmen, / from sons, friends, or wives, due to the complete worship of this liṅga.

Having slain thousands of wild beasts there along with his army and mounts, / the king, in pursuit of game, entered another forest.
Possessing pre-eminent strength, alone and afflicted with hunger and thirst, / having reached the end of the forest, he arrived at a vast wilderness.
Having passed through that as well, the ruler of men beheld an excellent hermitage / that caused delight to the mind and was exceedingly pleasing to the sight.
It was filled with flowering trees, with extremely pleasant meadows.
Then the long-armed [king], leaving behind his ministers, went there alone.
He did not see that seer of rigid vows in the hermitage.
He shouted aloud, as if making the forest resound: "Who is here?"

The king then spoke to the sweet-spoken maiden:

"O illustrious maiden, I have come to attend upon the best of sages.

6.2.m:
Where has the venerable one gone, fair lady? Tell me that, beautiful one."
Addressed thus by the king in that hermitage, the maiden,
laughing, replied with these sweet-toned words:

6.2.s:

tapasvino dhṛtimato dharmajñasya manasvinaḥ .. 15..

kaṇvaṃ hi pitaramanye pitaraṃ svamajānatī .. 16 ..
tasyāstadvacanaṃ śrutvā nṛpeṇoktaṃ varānane ..
suvyaktaṃ rājaputrī tvaṃ yathā kalyāṇi bhāṣase .. 17 ..

suvarṇaratnavāsāṃsi kuṃḍale parihārake .. 18 ..

gāṃdharveṇa ca māṃ bhīru vivāhenaiva suṃdari ..

nṛpasya vacanaṃ śrutvā kanyā vacanamabravīt ..

..rājovāca .. ..

tadarthaṃ māṃ sthitaṃ viddhi tvayā me'pahṛtaṃ manaḥ .. 21 ..
6.2.d:
कन्याहं पृथिवीपाल कौमारब्रह्मचारिणः ..
तपस्विनो धृतिमतो धर्मज्ञस्य मनस्विनः .. 15..
सुता कण्वस्य मामेवं विद्धि त्वं मनुजाधिप ..
कण्वं हि पितरमन्ये पितरं स्वमजानती .. 16 ..
तस्यास्तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा नृपेणोक्तं वरानने ..
सुव्यक्तं राजपुत्री त्वं यथा कल्याणि भाषसे .. 17 ..
भार्या मे भव सुश्रोणि ब्रूहि किं करवाणि ते ..
सुवर्णरत्नवासांसि कुंडले परिहारके .. 18 ..
आहरामि तवाद्याहं भार्या मे भव शोभने ..
गांधर्वेण च मां भीरु विवाहेनैव सुंदरि ..
विवाहानां च रंभोरु गांधर्वः श्रेष्ठ उच्यते .. 19 ..
नृपस्य वचनं श्रुत्वा कन्या वचनमब्रवीत् ..
मुहूर्त्तं संप्रतीक्षस्व स मां तुभ्यं प्रदास्यति .. 5.2.62.20 ..
..राजोवाच .. ..

तदर्थं मां स्थितं विद्धि त्वया मेऽपहृतं मनः .. 21 ..
6.2.m:
"O protector of the earth, I am the daughter of one who has been a celibate student from childhood,
an ascetic, steadfast, knower of righteousness, and wise.
Know me thus as the daughter of Kaṇva, O king of men.
For, not knowing my own father, I consider Kaṇva to be my father."
Hearing her words, [the king] said, O lovely-faced one:
"You are clearly a king's daughter, fair one, judging by the way you speak.
Become my wife, O woman of shapely hips! Tell me, what shall I do for you?
Gold, gems, garments, earrings, bracelets—
I bring them to you today; become my wife, beautiful one!
And marry me, timid girl, by the gāndharva marriage, beautiful one!
And of all marriages, O woman with thighs like plantain stems, the gāndharva is said to be the best."
Hearing the king's words, the maiden said this:
"Wait for a moment; he will bestow me upon you."
The king said:
"I desire you who are devoted to me, O blameless lady of lovely hips!
Know that I stand here for that purpose; my heart has been stolen away by you.

6.2.s:
ātmano baṃdhurātmaiva gatirātmaiva cātmanaḥ ..
ātmanaivātmano dānaṃ kartumarhasi dharmataḥ .. .. 22 ..
.. kanyovāca .. ..
yadi dharmapathastveṣa yadi cātmā prabhurmama ..

gāṃdharveṇa vivāhena kāmāsaktena pārvati .. 24 ..
kāmitā sā nṛpeṇeva tato gaṃtuṃ samudyataḥ ..
etasminnaṃtare devi kaṇvaścāśramamabhyagāt .. 25 ..
sā kanyā pitaraṃ dṛṣṭvā hriyā nopajagāma tam ..
vijñāyātha ca tāṃ vipro divyajñāno mahātapāḥ .. 26 ..

6.2.d:
आत्मनो बंधुरात्मैव गतिरात्मैव चात्मनः ..
आत्मनैवात्मनो दानं कर्तुमर्हसि धर्मतः .. .. 22 ..
.. कन्योवाच .. ..
यदि धर्मपथस्त्वेष यदि चात्मा प्रभुर्मम ..
सत्यं मे प्रतिजानीहि दत्तमात्मानमद्य मे .. 23 ..
इति तस्या वचः श्रुत्वा परिणीता नृपेण हि ..
गांधर्वेण विवाहेन कामासक्तेन पार्वति .. 24 ..
कामिता सा नृपेणेव ततो गंतुं समुद्यतः ..
एतस्मिन्नंतरे देवि कण्वश्चाश्रममभ्यगात् .. 25 ..
सा कन्या पितरं दृष्ट्वा ह्रिया नोपजगाम तम् ..
विज्ञायाथ च तां विप्रो दिव्यज्ञानो महातपाः .. 26 ..
उवाच परमं कुद्धस्तां कन्यां काममोहिताम् ..
त्वयापि दुष्टे रहसि मामवज्ञाय यत्कृतः .. 27 ..
स्वयं स्वयंवरो मोहात्तस्मात्कृष्णा भविष्यसि ..
कुत्सिता निर्घृणा दीना निर्लज्जा रूपवर्जिता .. 28 ..

6.2.m:
One's self alone is one's kinsman, and the self alone is one's refuge.
By yourself alone, according to dharma, you ought to make the gift of yourself."
The maiden said:
"If this indeed is the path of dharma, and if my self is my own master,
make a true promise to me; today my self is given to you."
Having heard her words, she was indeed wedded by the king,
by the gāndharva marriage, overwhelmed by desire, O Pārvatī.
Having enjoyed her, the king was about to depart;
meanwhile, O goddess, Kaṇva arrived at the hermitage.
Seeing her father, that maiden did not approach him out of shame.
Then, having understood her [state], the brahmin of divine knowledge and great austerity,
exceedingly enraged, said to that maiden deluded by passion:
"Since, O wicked girl, in secret, having disregarded me,
out of delusion you held your own svayaṃvara, therefore you shall become black,
repulsive, pitiless, miserable, shameless, and bereft of beauty!
This king, your husband, shall become deformed in appearance!"

6.2.s:
ityuktā tatkṣaṇājjātā sā kanyā rūpavarjitā ..
kurūpo nṛpatirjātaḥ śāpāttasya mahātmanaḥ .. 5.2.62.30 ..
atha prasādayāmāsa sā kanyā pitaraṃ tadā ..
bālānabhijñā mūḍhāhaṃ manmathena prapīḍitā .. 31 ..
ajñānācca kṛtaṃ pāpaṃ tāta tvaṃ kṣaṃtumarhasi ..
ayaṃ mahīpatistāta pratyaglīno mahāvrataḥ .. 32 ..
na cāhaṃ prārthitā tena mayāsau prārthito nṛpaḥ ..
tasmādanugrahaṃ tāta karttumarhasi cāvayoḥ .. 33 ..
iti tasyā vacaḥ śrutvā sa vipro'tikṛpānvitaḥ ..
uvāca svāṃ duhitaramāśvāsyaivaṃ punaḥpunaḥ .. 34 ..

akāryaṃ kārito yena balādahamaniṃdite ..
upadeśaṃ pradāsyāmi tattvaṃ kartumihārhasi .. 36 ..
mahākālavane puṇye liṃgaṃ rūpapradāyakam ..
paśupeśvarapūrve tu vidyate'bhīṣṭadāyakam ..37 ..
6.2.d:
इत्युक्ता तत्क्षणाज्जाता सा कन्या रूपवर्जिता ..
कुरूपो नृपतिर्जातः शापात्तस्य महात्मनः .. 5.2.62.30 ..
अथ प्रसादयामास सा कन्या पितरं तदा ..
बालानभिज्ञा मूढाहं मन्मथेन प्रपीडिता .. 31 ..
अज्ञानाच्च कृतं पापं तात त्वं क्षंतुमर्हसि ..
अयं महीपतिस्तात प्रत्यग्लीनो महाव्रतः .. 32 ..
न चाहं प्रार्थिता तेन मयासौ प्रार्थितो नृपः ..
तस्मादनुग्रहं तात कर्त्तुमर्हसि चावयोः .. 33 ..
इति तस्या वचः श्रुत्वा स विप्रोऽतिकृपान्वितः ..
उवाच स्वां दुहितरमाश्वास्यैवं पुनःपुनः .. 34 ..
नैव वागनृतं पुत्रि यावदद्य स्मराम्यहम् ..
दैवमत्र परं मन्ये धिग्बुद्धिं धिक्पराक्रमम् .. 35 ..
अकार्यं कारितो येन बलादहमनिंदिते ..
उपदेशं प्रदास्यामि तत्त्वं कर्तुमिहार्हसि .. 36 ..
महाकालवने पुण्ये लिंगं रूपप्रदायकम् ..
पशुपेश्वरपूर्वे तु विद्यतेऽभीष्टदायकम् ..37 ..
6.2.m:
Having been spoken to thus, that maiden instantly became bereft of beauty,
and the king became deformed through the curse of that great soul.
Then that maiden propitiated her father:
"I am a child, ignorant, foolish, afflicted by the god of love;
and out of ignorance a sin has been committed. O father, you should forgive me.
This lord of the earth, father, is noble and of great vows.
I was not wooed by him; rather, that king was wooed by me.
Therefore, father, you should grant grace to both of us."
Hearing her words, that brahmin, filled with great compassion,
consoling his daughter again and again, spoke thus:
"My word is never false, my daughter, as far back as I can recall today.
Here I consider destiny supreme; fie on intellect, fie on prowess,
by which I have been forcibly made to do what ought not to be done, O blameless girl!
I shall give you instructions; you should carry them out here.
In the sacred Mahākālavana there is a liṅga that grants beauty;
to the east of Paśupeśvara there is one that grants desires.

6.2.s:
tattvaṃ gaccha tvarā yuktā saha bhartrā nṛpeṇa hi ..
rūpaṃ prāpsyasi duṣprāpyaṃ liṃgadarśanamātrataḥ .. 38 ..
ityuktā sā tadā kanyā saha bhartrā gatā priye ..
mahākālavane ramye yatra liṃgamanuttamam .. 39 ..
dadarśa parayā bhaktyā sa ca rājā narottamaḥ ..
tatkṣaṇāddivyadehā sā rūpeṇātimanoharā ..
divyavastraparīdhānā divyālaṃkārabhūṣitā .. 5.2.62.40 ..
sa ca rājā tathā jātaḥ kaṃdarpasadṛśākṛtiḥ ..
rūpeṇāpratimo loke tasya liṃgasya darśanāt .. 41 ..
ato lokeṣu vikhyāto devo rūpeśvaraḥ priye ..
rūpado dhanado'tyarthaṃ putradaḥ svargadastathā .. 42 ..
sa ca rājā svakaṃ prāpto rāṣṭraṃ sasyādisaṃyutam ..
priyayā parayā sārdhaṃ cakre rājyamakaṃṭakam .. 43 ..
rājyaṃ kṛtvā gataḥ svargaṃ bhāryayā saha pārvati ..
dedīpyamāno vapuṣā dvitīya iva bhāskaraḥ .. 44 ..
6.2.d:
तत्त्वं गच्छ त्वरा युक्ता सह भर्त्रा नृपेण हि ..
रूपं प्राप्स्यसि दुष्प्राप्यं लिंगदर्शनमात्रतः .. 38 ..
इत्युक्ता सा तदा कन्या सह भर्त्रा गता प्रिये ..
महाकालवने रम्ये यत्र लिंगमनुत्तमम् .. 39 ..
ददर्श परया भक्त्या स च राजा नरोत्तमः ..
तत्क्षणाद्दिव्यदेहा सा रूपेणातिमनोहरा ..
दिव्यवस्त्रपरीधाना दिव्यालंकारभूषिता .. 5.2.62.40 ..
स च राजा तथा जातः कंदर्पसदृशाकृतिः ..
रूपेणाप्रतिमो लोके तस्य लिंगस्य दर्शनात् .. 41 ..
अतो लोकेषु विख्यातो देवो रूपेश्वरः प्रिये ..
रूपदो धनदोऽत्यर्थं पुत्रदः स्वर्गदस्तथा .. 42 ..
स च राजा स्वकं प्राप्तो राष्ट्रं सस्यादिसंयुतम् ..
प्रियया परया सार्धं चक्रे राज्यमकंटकम् .. 43 ..
राज्यं कृत्वा गतः स्वर्गं भार्यया सह पार्वति ..
देदीप्यमानो वपुषा द्वितीय इव भास्करः .. 44 ..
6.2.m:
Therefore, go in haste with your husband, the king.
You will regain beauty that is hard to attain, merely by the darśana of the liṅga."
Having been spoken to thus, that maiden went then with her husband, O beloved,
to the lovely Mahākālavana, where that unsurpassed liṅga is.
With supreme devotion she and that king, the best of men, beheld it.
At that very moment she gained a divine body, exceedingly charming in beauty.
wearing celestial garments and adorned with celestial ornaments. (40)
And the king likewise became one whose form resembled the god of love,
incomparable in beauty in the world, from the darśana of that liṅga. (41)
Therefore, O beloved, the god is renowned in the worlds as Rūpeśvara,
the bestower of beauty, the bestower of great wealth, the bestower of sons, and likewise the bestower of heaven. (42)
And the king reached his own realm, filled with crops and abundance,
and ruled his kingdom without any thorn [of adversity] alongside his beloved wife. (43)
Having ruled the kingdom, he went to heaven along with his wife, O Pārvatī,
shining brightly with his body like a second sun. (44)

6.2.s:

dhanavānrūpavānso'pi rājā bhavati bhūtale .. 5.2.62.50 ..

6.2.d:
विमानेन सुदीप्तेन वंद्यमानो दिवालये ..
दर्शनात्तस्य लिंगस्य प्राप्तः पदमनामयम् .. 45 ..
ये पश्यंति विशालाक्षि देवं रूपेश्वरं शिवम् ..
न ते रूपेण हीयंते यशसा च कुलेन च .. 46 ..
सदा रूपकरं लिंगं भुक्तिमुक्तिफलप्रदम् ..
ये पश्यंति वरारोहे तेषां लोकाः सदाऽक्षयाः .. 47 ..
येऽर्चयंति नरा नित्यं देवं रूपेश्वरं परम् ..
तेऽर्चिता यांति यानेन मम लोकं सनातनम् .. 48 ..
स एव सुकृती लोके कुलं तेनाप्यलंकृतम्..
यः पूजयति रूपेशं रूपसौभाग्यदायकम् .. 49 ..
यः पूजयति देवेशं प्रसंगादपि पार्वति ..
धनवान्रूपवान्सोऽपि राजा भवति भूतले .. 5.2.62.50 ..
एष ते कथितो देवि प्रभावः पापनाशनः ..
रूपेश्वरस्य देवस्य धनुःसाहस्रकं 7ब् .. 51 ..
6.2.m:
In a blazing aerial chariot, being praised in the abode of the gods,
he attained the state free from illness, through the darśana of that liṅga. (45)
Those who behold the god Rūpeśvara, Śiva, O large-eyed one,
do not fall away from beauty, fame, or noble family. (46)
Those who behold this liṅga which always grants beauty and bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation,
O fair-hipped one, their realms are forever imperishable. (47)
Those men who continually worship the supreme god Rūpeśvara,
worshipped themselves, go by [heavenly] vehicle to my eternal world. (48)
He alone is meritorious in this world, and by him his family is adorned,
whoever worships Rūpeśa, the bestower of beauty and good fortune. (49)
Whoever worships the lord of the gods, even by chance, O Pārvatī,
even he becomes a wealthy and beautiful king on the earth. (50)
This power that destroys sin has been told to you, O goddess,
of the god Rūpeśvara. [Now hear of] Dhanuḥsāhasraka. (51)

There he suddenly saw Madhusūdana lying asleep,
possessing the radiance of an autumn cloud, like a dark cloud in their midst.
Looking at him, he then spoke to the Daityas and his followers:
“This is that Madhusūdana, the thunderbolt to the mountains that are the Dānavas,
who decrees widowhood for the sportful wives that are the fame and arts of his enemies;
who destroys the decorative foliage on the cheeks of the lovely Daitya women;
this foremost foe who decrees widowhood for the bride that is our victory!
Free of doubt, he sleeps alone, forever of crooked intent.
This wicked one must be killed at once; he has come into view as desired!”

Īśvara said: / Know the sixty-sixth god, O beloved, to be Jalpeśvara, / by the mere darśana of whom even great sin goes to peace. / O great goddess, there was on earth a renowned king named Jalpa, / who was always devoted to debate, constantly initiating talk and argument, / full of speculations, always reflecting on the course of worldly existence. / To that king were born five mighty sons led by Subāhu, / who were like the five fires in bodily form, O woman of beautiful hips: / Subāhu, Śatrumardin, Jaya, and Vijaya, / and the fifth son was Vikrānta; all were masters of weapons and missiles.
They were established by their father, King Jalpa, in separate kingdoms.
Indeed, all those individual sons were made rulers over separate realms:
King Subāhu in the east, and Śatrumardana in the south,
King Jaya in the west, and King Vijaya in the north;
and the one named Vikrānta was placed in the middle, in his own position.
Having made such an arrangement, [the king] himself went to the forest.

6.2.m:
They had well-wishing ministers who had served by hereditary succession.
Then they enjoyed their respective kingdoms together with the ministers.
Now, the minister of Vikrānta, who was entirely devoted to doubts and schemes,
spoke to King Vikrānta in a solitary place:
"He who possesses this entire earth is proclaimed capable.
By exertion his station was obtained by the high-souled Vāsava.
And the nectar was obtained by the gods through exertion, O king.
Those men who are devoid of exertion, especially kṣatriyas,
they become objects of ridicule, their valour dwindling day by day.
And a brother, greedy for the kingdom, shows affection for the sake of wealth.
By that very strength of wealth, the king finds contentment.
Why, then, O king, is counsel not embraced?
Let the whole kingdom be enjoyed by me, your minister, by force.
Even a stranger who is beneficial is a kinsman; a kinsman who is harmful is a stranger.
Disease born in the body is harmful, while medicine from the forest is beneficial.
These devour the earth as snakes devour creatures living in holes:

Everything is deluded by illusion; who is a kinsman to whom?
Therefore, let an effort be made swiftly to subdue the brothers.
All brothers have been slain by brothers for the sake of a kingdom,
and, knowing the eternal duty, the asuras were slain by the gods."
Hearing this speech of the minister, that king was filled with amazement.
Smiling, he said in reply, "This enemy has come to me!"
Vikrānta said:
"We five brothers desire the earth.
Dissatisfied with separate dominions, how could the whole [earth] become [ours]?
Subāhu is the eldest brother, Śatrumardana is the second,
and Jaya and Vijaya—since I am the youngest among them."
The minister said:
"People honour the eldest who is established in the kingdom with excellent worshipful gifts.
What is this juniority and seniority among men who seek a kingdom?"
When it was agreed to, saying 'So be it', by King Vikrānta,

since I have become the cause of the destruction of the twice-born!
Those priests, carrying out the purpose of their master, of my sons,
perished; they were not wicked, but I am wicked, being the cause of destruction."
Thus with an agitated heart, that ruler of the earth, Jalpa,
bowed low and asked Vasiṣṭha again, the best of the wise:
The king said:
"O venerable one, tell me of a sacred ford that always prevents separation;
or, O brahmin, tell me of a liṅga, O lord, that immediately removes sin."
Hearing those words of his, of King Jalpa,
Vasiṣṭha declared by his divine knowledge, O Pārvatī:
"Go, Jalpa, by my command, to the supreme forest of Mahākāla,
where Rāma, having rid the earth of kṣatriyas, performs austerity.
There is a beginningless liṅga to the west of Kukkuṭeśvara.
Worship that, O king of kings, staying in the hermitage of Jāmadagnya."

6.2.m:
Having heard Vasiṣṭha's speech, that ruler of the earth, Jalpa,
left the Devadāru forest and went to the Mahākāla forest.
There he beheld that beginningless liṅga praised by the gods,
and worshipped it according to rule with supreme absorption.
There a voice arose from the midst of the liṅga, O lovely-faced one:
"You are not one of sinful conduct, nor are you the cause of death.
Unseen destiny was the cause in the case of the sons and the royal brahmins;
through the ripening of their own [karma] they have gone to the city of Vaivasvata.
Do not grieve, O king of kings; deep is the way of karma.
I am pleased with this pure disposition of yours, O best of kings;
name whatever boon you desire, and I will grant it to you without fail."
The king said:
"If you are pleased with me, O god, if a boon is to be granted to me:
may I have no rebirth in the terrible ocean of cyclic existence;
grant me imperishable renown, so that it becomes renowned on earth by my name:
'This lord is the god Jalpeśvara, worshipped by Jalpa.'

Let all the thirty [gods] say so; this is my boon, hard to attain.
Those mortals who behold you, who have become famous by my name—
may they suffer no separation from sons or from wealth;
let there be no fear of saṃsāra for them, nor from robbers, nor from the king;
let there never be fear from spirits, evil planets, or diseases.
May there be welfare forever for those to whose sight you have come;
they are blessed in the human world who have come to you for refuge.
Whatever merit is attained by men through ablutions at all sacred fords,
even more than all that is obtained, O god, by the sight of you.
They fall into the terrible cyclic existence, filled with hundreds of sorrows, only as long as
that god who ferries across the ocean of worldly existence is not seen.
When men have destroyed their sin, then sight of you is attained—
only through great merit, O lord, and not by meager austerity."
Having said, "So it shall be," O Pārvatī, by that liṅga,
he was drawn into its own body while all the gods looked on.

पिशाचत्वाद्विमुच्यंते स्वर्गं यांति न संशयः .. 5.2.68.50 ..
6.2.m: Those men who behold the [liṅga] named Piśāceśvara, O goddess— / their ancestors indeed, even those situated in hell, / are immediately freed from the condition of a piśāca and go to heaven, without a doubt.

6.2.s:
aśvamedhasya yajñasya samyagiṣṭasya yatphalam ..
tatphalaṃ labhate so'pi piśāceśvaradarśanāt .. 51 .
6.2.d:
अश्वमेधस्य यज्ञस्य सम्यगिष्टस्य यत्फलम् ..
तत्फलं लभते सोऽपि पिशाचेश्वरदर्शनात् .. 51 .
6.2.m: Whatever fruit is attained by the horse-sacrifice properly performed, / that fruit too one obtains from the darśana of Piśāceśvara.

6.2.s:
gayāyāṃ piṃḍadānena yatpuṇyaṃ samudāhṛtam..
tatpuṇyamadhikaṃ jñeyaṃ piśāceśvaradarśanāt .. 52..
6.2.d:
गयायां पिंडदानेन यत्पुण्यं समुदाहृतम्..
तत्पुण्यमधिकं ज्ञेयं पिशाचेश्वरदर्शनात् .. 52..
6.2.m: Whatever merit is spoken of by offering funeral cakes at Gayā, / that merit should be known to be exceeded by the darśana of Piśāceśvara.

6.2.s:
ye paśyaṃti caturdaśyāṃ piśāceśvarasaṃjñakam ..
pretatvaṃ ca piśācatvaṃ kule teṣāṃ na jāyate .. 53..
6.2.d:
ये पश्यंति चतुर्दश्यां पिशाचेश्वरसंज्ञकम् ..
प्रेतत्वं च पिशाचत्वं कुले तेषां न जायते .. 53..
6.2.m: Those who behold the [liṅga] named Piśāceśvara on the fourteenth [lunar day], / the state of a ghost or a piśāca is never born in their family.

6.2.s:
na viyoniṃ naro yāti narakaṃ ca na paśyati ..
prasaṃgenāpi yaḥ paśyetpiśāceśvarasaṃjñakam .. 54 ..
6.2.d:
न वियोनिं नरो याति नरकं च न पश्यति ..
प्रसंगेनापि यः पश्येत्पिशाचेश्वरसंज्ञकम् .. 54 ..
6.2.m: A man does not enter an animal womb, nor does he see hell, / if he should behold the [liṅga] named Piśāceśvara even by chance.

6.2.s:
sarvaiśvaryasamāyuktaḥ sarvabandhusamanvitaḥ ..
modate pitṛloke sa piśāceśvaradarśanāt .. 55 ..
6.2.d:
सर्वैश्वर्यसमायुक्तः सर्वबन्धुसमन्वितः ..
मोदते पितृलोके स पिशाचेश्वरदर्शनात् .. 55 ..
6.2.m: Endowed with all sovereignty, accompanied by all his kinsmen, / he rejoices in the world of the ancestors from the darśana of Piśāceśvara.

6.2.s:
kīrtanānmucyate pāpāddṛṣṭvā svargaṃ ca gacchati ..
sparśanādasya liṃgasya punātyāsaptamaṃ kulam.. 56 ..
6.2.d:
कीर्तनान्मुच्यते पापाद्दृष्ट्वा स्वर्गं च गच्छति ..
स्पर्शनादस्य लिंगस्य पुनात्यासप्तमं कुलम्.. 56 ..
6.2.m: By praising it one is freed from sin; by seeing it one goes to heaven; / by touching this liṅga, one purifies one's family up to the seventh generation.

6.2.s:
tadaiva sa naro muktaḥ saṃsāranigaḍādibhiḥ ..
yadaiva vīkṣate liṃgaṃ piśāceśvarasaṃjñakam .. 57 ..
6.2.d:
तदैव स नरो मुक्तः संसारनिगडादिभिः ..
यदैव वीक्षते लिंगं पिशाचेश्वरसंज्ञकम् .. 57 ..
6.2.m: At that very moment that man is freed from the shackles of worldly existence and the like, / at the very moment he beholds the liṅga named Piśāceśvara.

6.2.s:
yajñānāṃ tapasāṃ caiva dānānāṃ caiva yatphalam ..
tatphalaṃ koṭiguṇitaṃ jāyate tasya darśanāt .. 58..
6.2.d:
यज्ञानां तपसां चैव दानानां चैव यत्फलम् ..

6.2.m: Whatever is the fruit of sacrifices, austerities, and gifts, / that fruit becomes multiplied ten-millionfold from its darśana.

yadi paśyeccaturdaśyāṃ vaiśākhe kārttike tathā .
tasya puṇyamasaṃkhyātaṃ jāyate nātra saṃśayaḥ.. 59 ..
6.2.d:
यदि पश्येच्चतुर्दश्यां वैशाखे कार्त्तिके तथा .
तस्य पुण्यमसंख्यातं जायते नात्र संशयः.. 59 ..
6.2.m: If one should behold it on the fourteenth [lunar day] in the month of Vaiśākha or Kārttika, / one's merit becomes innumerable; there is no doubt about this.

6.2.s:
eṣa te kathito devi prabhāvaḥ pāpanāśanaḥ ..

6.2.d:
एष ते कथितो देवि प्रभावः पापनाशनः ..
पिशाचेश्वरदेवस्य श्रूयतां संगमेश्वरम् .. 5.2.68.60 ..
इति श्रीस्कांदे महापुराण एकाशीतिसाहस्र्यां संहितायां पञ्चम आवन्त्यखण्डे पिशाचेश्वरमाहात्म्यवर्णनंनामाष्टषष्टितमोऽध्यायः .. 68 . ...छ... ..
6.2.m:
This sin-destroying power of the divine Piśāceśvara has been told to you, O goddess; / now hear about Saṅgameśvara.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, named the description of the māhātmya of Piśāceśvara, in the fifth Avantī section of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, in the compendium of eighty-one thousand [verses].

6.2.m: Īśvara said: / Hear attentively, O goddess, about the lord named Piśāca, the sixty-eighth in number, / which destroys sins through darśana. (1) / In the beginning of the Kali age, O goddess, there was a very wealthy śūdra, / famous by the name of Soma, who was an atheist and a reviler of the Vedas, (2) / unfriendly to brahmins, cruel, miserly, shameless, / a betrayer of trust, and devoted to taking others' property. (3) / He destroyed the three goals of life of others and indulged his own desires; / one day, O goddess, he died with supreme agony. (4) / In the desert region he became a piśāca—naked, miserable, and terrifying, / a destroyer of piśācas, who wiped out his own kind. (5) / Many stronger piśācas were crushed by him. (6) / Then, along that very path, once came Śākaṭāyana, / devoted to sacred recitation, learned, eloquent, and dedicated to tranquility, (7) / resembling the rising sun, possessing splendor like fire; / traveling constantly in a cart, looking around, O Daughter of the Mountain, (8) / as he went along he saw that dreadful and terrifying piśāca. / Overcome by hunger, that piśāca ran up, desiring to devour him, (9) / having seen the brahmin Śākaṭāyana mounted upon the cart. / Hearing the sound of the cart and seeing the form of the twice-born, (5.2.68.10) / that piśāca was deafened in both ears; / intent on saving himself, he fled with difficulty, O Pārvatī. / Seeing him running away, the brahmin said to that piśāca: (11) / "O piśāca, you appear terrified and you seem in haste; / where are you running? Tell me, from where has your fear arisen?" (12) / The piśāca said: / "Hearing the terrifying roar of this great cart, / I have become deaf in both ears and senseless upon seeing you." (13) / The brahmin said: / "Brahmarākṣasas are heard to be the strongest among the piśācas; / you are a famous brahmarākṣasa desiring to devour me." (14) / The piśāca said:

6.2.m: "I am powerful among piśācas, yet I fled upon seeing you. / For death is sorrow for all, and life is exceedingly hard to obtain; / therefore, frightened, I run away for the sake of life and in search of well-being." (15) / The brahmin said: / "Whence is happiness for you, O piśāca? Death would indeed be better for you! / The state of a piśāca is a vile womb, born only to sinners." (16) / The piśāca said: / "For a living soul, wherever it goes, becomes a vessel of happiness; / therefore I desire to live. Be pleased, O brahmarākṣasa!" (17) / The brahmin said: / "I do not wish to devour you; I am a brahmin, not a rākṣasa! / I wander the earth for the welfare of all beings. (18) / A brahmin is said to be the friend of all living creatures; / do not fear me, for I have attained the disposition of a friend." (19) / Hearing his word, the piśāca, his mind reassured, / bowed down and replied thus to the brahmin Śākaṭāyana: (5.2.68.20) / "If you have granted the gift of fearlessness to all beings, / and if you have become friendly in deed, mind, and speech, (21) / I ask you, O fortunate one, a doubt lingering in my heart; / having heard it, you ought to explain it fully to me out of compassion: (22) / By what maturation of action does a human enter the state of a piśāca? / How is liberation from the condition of a piśāca attained by those of sinful deeds?" (23) / Hearing these words of that piśāca, O fair-faced one, / Śākaṭāyana, enveloped with affection, spoke to him: (24) / "Having stolen the property of a brahmin, and especially that of the gods, / through that sin the most sinful people enter the state of a piśāca. (25) / The man who, having deceived father, mother, wife, child, or a twice-born, / steals their wealth, becomes a piśāca. (26) / Having taken the king's property, he who neither sacrifices nor gives, / but nourishes only himself, goes to the state of a piśāca. (27) / Those who are betrayers of trust, and those who take delight in another's wife..."

6.2.m: "Those who revile the Vedas also attain the state of a piśāca. / Those men who always revile the Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras, / and who are ever slanderous, become piśācas. / Thus all this has now been told to you on the authority of the Vedas. / Now I will tell you who you were born as; listen to that: / You were a śūdra named Somaka, an exposer of others' secrets, / a betrayer of trust, a defamer of gods and brahmins, / an atheist who broke established norms, even in this seventh birth. / Having caused your family to fall exceedingly into terrible hell, / you have obtained the womb of a piśāca, and you will again go to Raurava, / to the hells named Mahāraurava, Krakaca, Kālasūtra, / the dreadful Yantrapīḍanaka, Mathana, and Kumbhavāluka." / As that brahmin was speaking thus, O illustrious one, / he remembered his own vile previous birth through association with the virtuous. / Overcome with grief, motionless, crying out repeatedly, "Fie! Fie!", / he fell to the ground, O goddess, and then spoke these words: / "Ah, by some merit I have obtained this sight of you— / I who have little merit, who am miserable and wretched! / There is no friend equal to dharma, there is no refuge equal to dharma, / there is no protection equal to dharma, and that dharma I do not possess, O lord! / I am drowned in the ocean of sorrow, I am sunk in the mire of sin; / I have wandered in blinding darkness; therefore I have taken refuge in you! / Reverence to you, O noble one! What should I do? Instruct me! / That which was ordained by the power of austerities has now been attained by me." / As that piśāca was speaking thus, O fair-faced lady, / that learned brahmin Śākaṭāyana related the māhātmya: / "Whatever sacred fords there are on earth extending to the ocean, / and whatever sacred fields exist here, superior in granting great merit to them / is the sacred field Mahākālavana, which remains indestructible even at the cosmic dissolution.

6.2.m:
Because of mutual affection, there was supreme love between the two. / But in that king, a headache always arose at midday.
By the foremost knowers of Āyurveda, the physicians of the body,
prescriptions were applied, O dear one, yet the pain increased day by day.
When a very long time had passed in this manner, O goddess, the king
was addressed by the large-eyed [queen], distressed by her husband's suffering:
"How is it that this affliction of a headache [wears you down], O lord of the earth?
And many physicians, O lord, skilled in various treatises,
strive for its destruction, yet it is still not alleviated?"
Being spoken to in this manner by his beloved, Subāhu, the lord of the earth,
replied with affection to his dear wife, who was tender with love:
"O goddess, the body of all embodied beings is the abode of pleasure and pain.
Pleasure and pain arise in accordance with past actions. (9)
Though addressed in this way by that king, O fair-faced lady,
the queen, deeply distressed, spoke again on that very matter with deep affection: (10)
When, though restrained repeatedly, she kept asking again and again,

the king smiled and said to the queen: (11)
“If you wish to hear the origin of this illness
and its cause in truth, O queen, I will not speak of it here. (12)
Having gone to the Mahākāla forest, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
there I will tell you, if you have curiosity. (13)
Tomorrow at dawn I shall go along with you, O lady of bright smiles.”
Hearing his words, the queen stood astonished,
eager to depart for the auspicious Mahākāla forest. (14)
Then that night passed; at dawn the best of kings
set out together with his wife, surrounded by a large army. (15)
In due course he reached the auspicious Mahākāla forest;
the wise king then made his encampment on the bank of the Śiprā. (16)
There is the Gaṅgā flowing to Pātāla, traversing the three paths,
and the second, the Nīlagaṅgā, joined with the Śiprā. (17)
Their confluence is there, where stands that liṅga Saṅgameśvara,
worshipped alongside the Gaṅgā, the Śiprā, and the Nīlagaṅgā. (18)

6.2.m:
Now when Subāhu arrived, the queen, filled with wonder
and moved by love, asked: “Let the cause be told here,
as was said by you before, O king: ‘I will tell you there.’” (19)
Being thus addressed by his beloved, the king Subāhu
smiled repeatedly and replied to his beloved with affection: (20)
“Sleep comfortably, O fair-limbed, blameless lady; we are tired.
At dawn I will tell the cause of the head disease.” (21)
Then that night passed; at dawn the best of kings
recounted the māhātmya of the supreme lord: (22)
“I was a wicked Śūdra, constantly reviling the Vedas,
always a betrayer of trust; and you too were of the same sort. (23)
A son was born, ill-behaved, a deceiver of gods and brahmins,
deformed, harsh, wicked, an evil man by nature. (24)
Then, after a long time, a dreadful drought of twelve years occurred,
causing terror to all living creatures. (25)
A separation took place between you, myself, and our son.

6.2.m:
Then, tormented by sorrow, I attained supreme dispassion. (26)
Desiring immediate death, these words were spoken by me:
‘For me, devoid of merit and intent on evil contemplation, (27)
reunion with my wife and son is hard to attain again.
How can a sinner sleep after committing dreadful sin? (28)
He acts merely for the sake of his family, but he must cross over alone.
Dharma alone is the supreme kinsman; dharma alone is the supreme goal.
Everything is accomplished by dharma; therefore one should take refuge in dharma.’ (29)
While deeply contemplating thus, O beloved, my life-breaths departed.
Various torments were experienced by me in ten million hells. (30)
By that merit of praising dharma even at the time of death,
I was born as a fish in the auspicious waters of the Śiprā. (31)
And you were then born as a female hawk in that very excellent forest.
Then, when the rainy season arrived and the sun entered Āśleṣā, (32)
I was carried out of the water by the rush of the three rivers.

6.2.m:
I was seized by the head by you and pierced with talons, O lovely lady. (33)
I was carried by you, O queen, into the presence of Saṅgameśvara;
death was met by you along with me at the hands of fishermen, O fair-faced lady. (34)
As I was dying, that lord Saṅgameśvara was seen by me,
bathed abundantly by the Śiprā, the Gaṅgā, and the Nīlagaṅgā. (35)
Merely by the darśana of him, I was born as a king
in the realm of Kaliṅga, O queen, revered by all monarchs. (36)
You were born as the beloved daughter of Dṛḍhadhanvan, an inhabitant of Kāñcīpura
devoted to the duty of the warrior class, a fortunate woman. (37)
We two attained kingship through the sight of that liṅga.
I was pierced by you with claws and killed with those clubs.
Remembering that destruction at midday, pain then arose in my head.
I remember my own birth through the sight of this god.
This has been told to you, O goddess, as I was asked by you formerly.
Go, fair woman, may you have good fortune, wherever your heart wishes to go.

And I must remain right here; this Saṃgameśvara must be served.”
Then she of flawless limbs, with eyes like blue lotuses,
making her sweet voice plaintive, spoke this to her husband:
“O lord, I too remembered what was done in my previous birth.
By the power of this liṅga, although fallen into animal wombs,
we two obtained human birth, and that in stainless families;
peerless royal splendour was obtained in the world, an unthwarted kingdom was obtained.
I was gained as your beloved wife, and you were gained by me, O king.
He is renowned in the three worlds by the name of Saṃgameśvara.
By the power of this god, there will be no separation,
just as for Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī, and for Pārvatī and Śiva.”
Bowing down again, submissive, agitated suddenly by passion, [she said:]
“May Subāhu be my husband in another birth in this world,
by the grace of you, O god, if you are indeed Saṃgameśvara!”
Then, beholding her who had blossomed, rippling with the god of love,

6.2.m:
as if drinking in his beloved with his gaze, he spoke to the tremulous-eyed woman:
“Adorned with noble birth, natural virtues, and beauty,
you have been won by me, O large-eyed woman; the fruit of my birth has been obtained.”
Then, taking that beloved by the hand—terrified with fear,
with trembling blossom-like lower lip—he went to his inner apartments,
saying, “I am bitten by the serpent of love now by fate.”
He moved about there, realizing in his mind that worldly existence is substanceless.
O woman of lovely hips, he took delight with her for a long time in my city.
Thus the king, having obtained his beloved and related his story,
enjoyed the kingdom along with her, expanding great festivities.
Knowing this world to be impermanent, he also gave wealth to supplicants.
Because of that unprecedented generosity of his, the three worlds were astonished.
Having ruled the kingdom for a long time together with his wife, that best of kings,
and having enjoyed abundant pleasures, attained dissolution in that liṅga.
Therefore, O goddess, that god is celebrated as Saṃgameśvara.

6.2.m:
Whoever sees that liṅga Saṃgameśvara with supreme devotion
will have no separation from sons, brothers, beloved ones, and the like.
He who regularly beholds that liṅga Saṃgameśvara,
for him the fruit will be greater than that of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
The merit associated with the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Narmadā, / and the Candrabhāgā becomes fruitful through the sight of Saṃgameśvara.
Whoever sees that liṅga Saṃgameśvara in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
by him the pilgrimage to Kārtikasvāmin has been performed, without a doubt.
Whoever sees the god Saṃgameśvara in the month of Āśvayuja,
by him a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices have been performed, O fair-faced woman.
Whoever sees that liṅga Saṃgameśvara in the month of Kārttika, / a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices have been performed by him, without a doubt.

6.2.m:
Īśvara said:
Know the seventy-first to be called Prayāgeśvara; / know it to be incomparable, destroying heinous sins. (1)
In the city of Hāstina there was a fortunate and supreme king, Śaṃtanu, / in the Vaivasvata interval of the kalpa, during the age called Dvāpara. (2)
He possessed wondrous great prowess, a youth of adamantine build, / skilled in all sacred sciences, knowledgeable in the host of arts, (3)
equal to Viṣṇu in strength, and like the sun in splendour. / He wandered alone along the Gaṅgā, which is frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas. (4)
Once that mighty-armed king, possessing abundant troops and mounts, / entered the dense forest surrounded by hundreds of horses and elephants. (5)
Having gone there, the best of kings killed deer and tigers sportively, / striking down buffaloes, wild horses, and boars. (6)
Once in that forest he saw a superb woman / blazing with her body, just like a visible second Padmā. (7)
Seeing her, his hair stood on end, amazed by her wealth of beauty; / as if drinking her in with both eyes, the lord of men was not satiated. (8)
And as soon as she saw the king of great splendour roaming about, / that charming woman, filled with love and affection, was not satiated. (9)
Then the king addressed her, soothing her with gentle words: / "Are you a goddess, a Dānavī, a Gandharvī, or an apsaras, (10)
or a Yakṣī, a serpent maiden, or a human woman, O slender-waisted lady? / I beseech you who resemble the interior of a lotus: become my wife, O beautiful one!" (11)
Having heard these words of the king, praised, soft, and lovely, / it was accepted by her, O goddess, and a stipulation was requested of the king: (12)
"If I am prevented or treated with displeasure, I shall certainly abandon you. / You must never ask, O king: 'Who are you and whose are you?'" (13)
"So be it," said he, with truthfulness and virtue. / By her conduct and character, her beauty, generosity, and virtues, (14)
and by her attentions in private, the lord of the earth was delighted. / For she was of divine form, the goddess Gaṅgā, the river flowing along three paths. (15)

6.2.m:
Having assumed a human form, radiant one, O lady of excellent complexion, / she brought delight to the king, and took delight in him as well. (16)
Attached to amorous pleasure and captivated by the excellent qualities of women, / the king did not notice the passing of many years, seasons, and months. (17)
Sporting with her at his pleasure, the ruler of men / begot upon her eight sons who possessed immortal complexion. (18)
As each son was born, she threw him into the water for his liberation, / saying, "I please you," into the purifying current of the Gaṅgā. (19)
That was not pleasing to King Śaṃtanu at all; / yet the lord of the earth said nothing to that goddess, terrified of abandonment. (20)
Then, as the eighth son was born and she seemed to smile, / the king, afflicted with grief and wishing to protect his son, said: (21)
"Do not kill him! Whose are you and who are you? Why do you destroy your sons? / Slaying a son is a great sin; do not incur it, stay, O blameworthy woman!" (22)
Gaṅgā said:
"O best of those who have sons, desiring a son as you do, I shall not kill your son. / But my stay here has come to an end, according to the agreement made by me. (23)
I am Gaṅgā, the daughter of Jahnu, attended by hosts of great seers; / I have dwelt with you for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. (24)
These are the eight Vasu gods, very terrible and of great splendour; / by the flaw of Vasiṣṭha's curse they entered into human state. (25)
Other than you, no bringer of them exists on the earth, / and a human mother such as I could never exist. (26)
Therefore, for the sake of being their mother, I have assumed human state. / May welfare be yours; I shall depart. Protect your son, O king of great vows!" (27)
Having spoken thus, Gaṅgā, deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu, / wept, having resorted to human nature, that slender-waisted lady: (28)
"Oh, alas, what great misery that these sons were killed! / By me, cruel through delusion, the infants were cast into the water. (29)
Alas, my children! Alas, my sons! Where indeed are my dear boys?"

6.2.m: "Where have they gone, leaving me? Why does my heart not burst? / Calling out plaintively, 'Mother! Mother!', coming of their own accord, / when, embracing those sons in affection, crying, 'My child! My child!'— / by whom, coated with tawny dust of the earth, / will my upper garment and lap ever be soiled? / Born from each and every limb, delighting mind and heart, / alas, my children have been killed, sent to death by me, their mother! / What worlds shall I go to after committing such a dreadful deed? / How shall I, a merciless slayer of sons, ever become pure?" / Lameneting piteously thus, weeping again and again, / she fainted and fell to the ground, distressed and motionless. / In the meantime, O goddess, Nārada, the best of sages, / suddenly heard that sound of her lamentation. / With eyes wide with wonder, he thought: "What is this? / This is that Gaṅgā, born of Jahnu, purifier, praised by the gods, / the divine chief queen of the ocean, the sacred three-pathed river; / having assumed human nature, why does she weep so wildly?" / Thinking thus, the sage approached; / Nārada, the son of Brahmā, standing in the sky, said loudly to the weeping Gaṅgā: / "O goddess Gaṅgā, obeisance to you! / I am Nārada, O most holy one. Why do you weep, O purifier? / You are renowned as the daughter of the snowy mountain, attended by gods and gandharvas, / borne on the head by the god Śiva, the Supreme Lord." / Hearing Nārada's words, the divine river of the gods, / beholding him situated in his aerial chariot, replied to the great sage: / "O Nārada, through delusion I have committed a reprehensible unrighteousness; / knowing full well it was a great sin, seven sons were killed by me. / Separation from the ocean befell me by fate; / I became the wife of a mortal; sons were born to me and were slain. / Therefore I lament, submerged in an ocean of grief.

6.2.m: Tell me, O divine seer, how I may indeed become pure." / Hearing these words of hers, Nārada, the best of sages, / who knows the three times and is pure-souled, spoke to Gaṅgā: / Nārada said: / "O you praised by the world, have you forgotten the auspicious agreement with the gods, / which was promised by you, O goddess, for the liberation of the Vasus? / Those Vasus have attained their realms by your grace, O faithful one! / The ocean, called Śaṃtanu, was brought down [to earth] by you, O goddess." / Hearing these words of the noble Nārada, / holy Gaṅgā, the three-pathed river, replied to the great sage: / "You have spoken the truth, O brahmin; now I know everything. / But because a human womb was taken, I was bewildered by it. / Terrified of the fear of infamy, I have taken refuge in you. / Give me instruction; tell me of an excellent place." / Nārada said: / "O you praised by the world, is the agreement made with the gods forgotten? / If, terrified of the fear of infamy, O goddess who bestows merit, / you ask me for an ultimate place, listen, O faithful one, I shall tell you. / Avantī is renowned, eternal through seven kalpas; / in it is your friend Śiprā, who is always dear to brahmins. / On its bank, to the south of Durdharṣeśvara, is an auspicious liṅga, / worthy of worship by the thirty [gods] and attended by all sacred fords. / Merely by its darśana, you will have accomplished your purpose. / Therefore, go, O most holy Gaṅgā, attended by divine seers!" / Thus addressed by the noble Nārada, the most holy three-pathed river / went there and beheld her friend Śiprā. / Then, embracing her and beholding the supremely purifying liṅga, / she worshipped it with devotion and remained right there for a long time. / Then the goddess Yamunā, daughter of the sun, destroyer of sin, / came there with affection to where Gaṅgā was staying.

6.2.m: The goddess beheld Gaṅgā meditating on Śiva, Śaṃkara. / She too remained right there, worshipping supreme Śiva. / Then, at that very time, goddess Sarasvatī, flowing eastward, / arrived, deeply concealed, in the waters of Gaṅgā and Yamunā. / Meanwhile, O goddess, Nārada said to Śakra: / "Prayāga is not seen; it has gone to the forest of Mahākāla. / Where Sarasvatī is concealed between Gaṅgā and Yamunā, / that is to be known as Prayāga, destroyer of all sins. / That Prayāga is now in the excellent forest of Mahākāla; / for what reason it has gone, I do not know." / Hearing these words of the noble Nārada, / all [the gods], accompanied by Śakra, came to Avantī, / praising the auspicious, three-pathed Gaṅgā with various hymns: / "O goddess Gaṅgā, obeisance to you, destroyer of all sins, / mother of the Vasus, O goddess, granter of liberation to the Vasus, / ever the purifier of the three worlds, borne on the head by Hara! / Attended by the Vālakhilyas, the supreme part of Kṛṣṇa, / O Yamunā, Kālindī, river of boons, we bow to you! / You are the purifying daughter of Mārtaṇḍa, lord of the sky. / O goddess Śiprā, born from the body of Brahmā, auspicious one, obeisance to you! / You alone are renowned as the eastward-flowing Sarasvatī of holy form; / that which flows eastward in the sacred field of the Kurus, at Puṣkara, and at Mahālaya, / you, that very same renowned Śiprā, are the destroyer of all wicked deeds. / You are compassion to all beings, heaven, and refuge to mortals; / you are the mother of all beings; you are sung on earth as the eastward-flowing. / Seeing the stain and mark of many births of embodied beings on earth, / you wash it away, O goddess; such are you, abiding in the three worlds. / The confluence of these [rivers] is remembered by the wise as Prayāga. / Having arrived here, it is now established and bathed by you."
